# Page: Objective Function Evaluation

# Objective Function Evaluation

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [src/comprest.f90](src/comprest.f90)
- [src/computef.f90](src/computef.f90)
- [src/computeg.f90](src/computeg.f90)
- [src/fparc.f90](src/fparc.f90)
- [src/gparc.f90](src/gparc.f90)
- [src/gwalls.f90](src/gwalls.f90)

</details>



## Purpose and Scope

This page describes how Packmol computes the objective function value and its gradient during the optimization process. The objective function quantifies how well molecules are packed, balancing two competing goals: maintaining minimum distances between atoms and satisfying geometric constraints.

The objective function evaluation is invoked by the GENCAN optimization solver (see [Optimization Engine (GENCAN)](#4.4)) and relies on spatial data structures documented in [Spatial Management System](#4.5). For details on individual atom-pair interactions, see [Atom-to-Atom Interactions](#4.7). For constraint system details, see [Constraint System Implementation](#7.2).

## Objective Function Structure

The objective function `f(x)` consists of two main components that are summed together:

| Component | Symbol | Description | Scale Factor |
|-----------|--------|-------------|--------------|
| **Distance Penalties** | `fdist` | Quadratic penalties when atoms are closer than their combined radii | `fscale(i)*fscale(j)` |
| **Constraint Penalties** | `frest` | Penalties for violating geometric constraints (inside/outside regions) | `scale` or `scale2` |

```
f(x) = Σ fdist(i,j) + Σ frest(i)
```

The optimization succeeds when `f(x)` approaches zero, indicating all distance requirements and constraints are satisfied.

**Sources:** [src/computef.f90:1-154](), [src/compute_data.f90]()

## Function Evaluation Overview

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    GENCAN["GENCAN Solver"] --> COMPUTEF["computef(n, x, f)<br/>src/computef.f90"]
    GENCAN --> COMPUTEG["computeg(n, x, g)<br/>src/computeg.f90"]
    
    COMPUTEF --> RESET1["Reset f=0, frest=0, fdist=0"]
    RESET1 --> RESETCELLS1["resetcells()<br/>Clear cell data"]
    RESETCELLS1 --> TRANSFORM1["Transform x to Cartesian<br/>xcm + Euler angles → xcart"]
    
    TRANSFORM1 --> COMPREST["comprest(icart, fplus)<br/>Evaluate constraints"]
    TRANSFORM1 --> BUILD_CELLS1["Build cell linked lists<br/>latomfirst, lcellfirst"]
    
    BUILD_CELLS1 --> FPARC["fparc(icart, firstjcart)<br/>Distance penalties"]
    COMPREST --> SUM_F["Sum contributions to f"]
    FPARC --> SUM_F
    
    COMPUTEG --> RESET2["Reset gxcar(:,:)=0"]
    RESET2 --> RESETCELLS2["resetcells()<br/>Clear cell data"]
    RESETCELLS2 --> TRANSFORM2["Transform x to Cartesian<br/>xcm + Euler angles → xcart"]
    
    TRANSFORM2 --> GWALLS["gwalls(icart, irest)<br/>Constraint gradients"]
    TRANSFORM2 --> BUILD_CELLS2["Build cell linked lists"]
    
    BUILD_CELLS2 --> GPARC["gparc(icart, firstjcart)<br/>Distance gradients"]
    GWALLS --> CHAIN_RULE["Apply chain rule<br/>gxcar → g"]
    GPARC --> CHAIN_RULE
    
    style COMPUTEF fill:#ffe6e6
    style COMPUTEG fill:#e6f3ff
    style FPARC fill:#ffffcc
    style GPARC fill:#ffffcc
```

**Sources:** [src/computef.f90:9-154](), [src/computeg.f90:9-244]()

## Function Value Computation (computef)

The `computef` subroutine in [src/computef.f90:9-154]() evaluates the objective function value through the following steps:

### Step 1: Coordinate Transformation

The optimization variables `x` are in **generalized coordinates**: center-of-mass positions and Euler angles (β, γ, θ) for each molecule. These must be converted to **Cartesian coordinates** for all atoms.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "Generalized Coordinates (x)"
        XCM["x(1:3*ntotmol)<br/>Center of mass<br/>xcm for each molecule"]
        ANGLES["x(3*ntotmol+1:6*ntotmol)<br/>Euler angles<br/>beta, gama, teta"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Transformation"
        EULER["eulerrmat(beta, gama, teta, v1, v2, v3)<br/>Compute rotation matrix"]
        COMPCART["compcart(xcart, xcm, coor, v1, v2, v3)<br/>xcart = xcm + R * coor"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Cartesian Coordinates"
        XCART["xcart(icart, 1:3)<br/>Cartesian position<br/>for each atom"]
    end
    
    XCM --> COMPCART
    ANGLES --> EULER
    EULER --> COMPCART
    COMPCART --> XCART
```

The loops in [src/computef.f90:44-109]() iterate over molecule types and molecules, computing Cartesian coordinates and simultaneously building cell data structures:

```
ilubar = 0                  ! Index for center-of-mass coordinates
ilugan = ntotmol*3          ! Index for angle coordinates
icart = 0                   ! Atom counter

for each molecule type:
  for each molecule:
    xcm = x(ilubar+1:ilubar+3)
    beta, gama, teta = x(ilugan+1:ilugan+3)
    
    for each atom in molecule:
      icart = icart + 1
      xcart(icart,:) = xcm + R(beta,gama,teta) * coor(idatom,:)
```

**Sources:** [src/computef.f90:40-109](), [src/eulerrmat.f90](), [src/compcart.f90]()

### Step 2: Constraint Evaluation

For each atom, the subroutine `comprest` evaluates all geometric constraints applied to that atom:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    ATOM["Atom icart<br/>xcart(icart, 1:3)"]
    ATOM --> LOOP["Loop over nratom(icart)<br/>constraints"]
    
    LOOP --> TYPE2["ityperest=2<br/>Inside Cube"]
    LOOP --> TYPE3["ityperest=3<br/>Inside Box"]
    LOOP --> TYPE4["ityperest=4<br/>Outside Sphere"]
    LOOP --> TYPE5["ityperest=5<br/>Outside Ellipsoid"]
    LOOP --> TYPE6["ityperest=6<br/>Outside Cube"]
    LOOP --> TYPE10["ityperest=10<br/>Above Plane"]
    LOOP --> TYPE12["ityperest=12<br/>Inside Cylinder"]
    LOOP --> MORE["... 15 constraint types"]
    
    TYPE2 --> PENALTY["Compute penalty fplus<br/>if constraint violated"]
    TYPE3 --> PENALTY
    TYPE4 --> PENALTY
    TYPE5 --> PENALTY
    TYPE6 --> PENALTY
    TYPE10 --> PENALTY
    TYPE12 --> PENALTY
    MORE --> PENALTY
    
    PENALTY --> SUM["f = f + fplus<br/>frest = max(frest, fplus)"]
```

The penalty formulas are quadratic. For example, for an "inside cube" constraint ([src/comprest.f90:29-44]()):
- If `xcart(icart,1) < xmin`, penalty includes `scale * (xcart - xmin)²`
- If `xcart(icart,1) > xmax`, penalty includes `scale * (xcart - xmax)²`

**Sources:** [src/computef.f90:76-79](), [src/comprest.f90:11-215]()

### Step 3: Cell Construction and Distance Evaluation

After transforming all atoms to Cartesian coordinates, the code builds cell-based spatial data structures ([src/computef.f90:83-101]()):

```
call setcell(xcart(icart,:), cell)           ! Determine cell indices
latomnext(icart) = latomfirst(i,j,k)         ! Link atom into cell
latomfirst(i,j,k) = icart
if (empty_cell(i,j,k)) then
  empty_cell(i,j,k) = .false.
  lcellnext(icell) = lcellfirst              ! Link cell into occupied list
  lcellfirst = icell
end if
```

Distance penalties are then computed by iterating over occupied cells and checking neighboring cells ([src/computef.f90:115-151]()):

```mermaid
graph TD
    START["lcellfirst"] --> CELL_LOOP["Loop over occupied cells<br/>icell → cell(i,j,k)"]
    
    CELL_LOOP --> ATOM_LOOP["Loop over atoms in cell<br/>icart = latomfirst(i,j,k)"]
    
    ATOM_LOOP --> SELF["fparc(icart, latomnext(icart))<br/>Same cell"]
    ATOM_LOOP --> FACE1["fparc(icart, latomfirst(i+1,j,k))<br/>Forward face neighbors"]
    ATOM_LOOP --> FACE2["fparc(icart, latomfirst(i,j+1,k))"]
    ATOM_LOOP --> FACE3["fparc(icart, latomfirst(i,j,k+1))"]
    ATOM_LOOP --> EDGE1["fparc(icart, latomfirst(i+1,j-1,k))<br/>Forward edge neighbors"]
    ATOM_LOOP --> EDGE2["fparc(icart, latomfirst(i+1,j,k-1))"]
    ATOM_LOOP --> CORNER["fparc(icart, latomfirst(i+1,j+1,k+1))<br/>Forward corner neighbors"]
    ATOM_LOOP --> MORE["... 14 neighbor cells total"]
    
    SELF --> SUM_F["f = f + penalty"]
    FACE1 --> SUM_F
    FACE2 --> SUM_F
    FACE3 --> SUM_F
    EDGE1 --> SUM_F
    EDGE2 --> SUM_F
    CORNER --> SUM_F
    MORE --> SUM_F
    
    SUM_F --> NEXT_ATOM["latomnext(icart)"]
    NEXT_ATOM --> ATOM_LOOP
    ATOM_LOOP --> NEXT_CELL["lcellnext(icell)"]
    NEXT_CELL --> CELL_LOOP
```

The 14-cell neighbor search pattern examines the atom's own cell plus 13 forward neighbors to avoid double-counting pairs. This reduces O(N²) pairwise checks to O(N).

**Sources:** [src/computef.f90:115-151](), [src/cell_indexing.f90]()

## Distance Penalty Function (fparc)

The `fparc` function in [src/fparc.f90:10-77]() computes distance penalties for atom pairs. For each pair (icart, jcart):

### Pairwise Distance Computation

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    PAIR["Atom pair (icart, jcart)"]
    
    PAIR --> CHECK1["Skip if same molecule"]
    PAIR --> CHECK2["Skip if both fixed"]
    PAIR --> CHECK3["Skip if type not computed"]
    
    CHECK1 --> DIST["vdiff = delta_vector(xcart(i), xcart(j), pbc_length)<br/>datom = vdiff² (squared distance)"]
    CHECK2 --> DIST
    CHECK3 --> DIST
    
    DIST --> TOL["tol = (radius(i) + radius(j))²"]
    TOL --> COMPARE["datom < tol?"]
    
    COMPARE -->|Yes| PENALTY["penalty = fscale(i)*fscale(j)*(datom - tol)²"]
    COMPARE -->|No| NO_PENALTY["No penalty"]
    
    PENALTY --> SHORT_CHECK["use_short_radius?"]
    SHORT_CHECK -->|Yes| SHORT_TOL["short_tol = (short_radius(i) + short_radius(j))²"]
    SHORT_TOL --> SHORT_COMPARE["datom < short_tol?"]
    SHORT_COMPARE -->|Yes| SHORT_PENALTY["Additional penalty<br/>short_tol_scale*(datom - short_tol)²"]
    SHORT_COMPARE -->|No| RETURN
    SHORT_PENALTY --> RETURN["Return total penalty"]
    SHORT_CHECK -->|No| RETURN
    NO_PENALTY --> RETURN
```

The penalty formula is:

```
if datom < tol:
  penalty = fscale(i) * fscale(j) * (datom - tol)²
  
  if datom < short_tol:
    penalty += fscale(i) * fscale(j) * short_tol_scale * (datom - short_tol)²
```

This creates a smooth quadratic penalty that increases as atoms get closer. The short radius system (see [Radius and Tolerance System](#7.3)) adds extra penalties for extremely close atoms.

**Sources:** [src/fparc.f90:10-77](), [src/pbc.f90]()

## Gradient Computation (computeg)

The `computeg` subroutine in [src/computeg.f90:9-244]() computes the gradient `g` of the objective function with respect to the generalized coordinates `x`. The process mirrors `computef` but accumulates gradients instead of function values.

### Cartesian Gradient Accumulation

The gradient computation proceeds in two phases:

**Phase 1: Compute gradients in Cartesian space** ([src/computeg.f90:32-143]()):

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    RESET["gxcar(:,:) = 0"]
    RESET --> TRANSFORM["Transform x to xcart<br/>(same as computef)"]
    
    TRANSFORM --> GWALLS_CALL["For each atom icart:<br/>For each constraint irest:<br/>gwalls(icart, irest)"]
    TRANSFORM --> BUILD_CELLS["Build cell linked lists"]
    
    BUILD_CELLS --> GPARC_CALL["For each atom icart:<br/>For 14 neighbor cells:<br/>gparc(icart, firstjcart)"]
    
    GWALLS_CALL --> GXCAR["gxcar(icart, 1:3)<br/>Gradient w.r.t. Cartesian coords"]
    GPARC_CALL --> GXCAR
```

Both `gwalls` and `gparc` accumulate contributions into the array `gxcar(icart, k)`, which stores ∂f/∂xcart for each atom's Cartesian coordinates.

**Phase 2: Transform to generalized coordinates using chain rule** ([src/computeg.f90:145-241]()):

```
g(1:n) = 0

for each molecule:
  for each atom in molecule:
    // Center-of-mass gradient: direct copy
    g(k1+1:k1+3) += gxcar(icart, 1:3)
    
    // Angle gradients: chain rule
    g(k2+1) += Σ_k coor(idatom, :) · dv1beta(k) * gxcar(icart, k)
    g(k2+2) += Σ_k coor(idatom, :) · dv1gama(k) * gxcar(icart, k)
    g(k2+3) += Σ_k coor(idatom, :) · dv1teta(k) * gxcar(icart, k)
```

**Sources:** [src/computeg.f90:9-244]()

## Chain Rule for Angle Gradients

The transformation from Cartesian gradients to angle gradients uses the chain rule. Since:

```
xcart = xcm + R(β,γ,θ) * coor
```

The gradient with respect to angles requires computing derivatives of the rotation matrix:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "Cartesian Gradient"
        GXCAR["gxcar(icart, k)<br/>∂f/∂xcart_k"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Rotation Matrix Derivatives"
        DV1BETA["dv1beta, dv2beta, dv3beta<br/>∂R/∂β"]
        DV1GAMA["dv1gama, dv2gama, dv3gama<br/>∂R/∂γ"]
        DV1TETA["dv1teta, dv2teta, dv3teta<br/>∂R/∂θ"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Chain Rule"
        CHAIN["∂f/∂angle = Σ_k (∂f/∂xcart_k) * (∂xcart_k/∂angle)"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Angle Gradients"
        G_BETA["g(k2+1) = ∂f/∂β"]
        G_GAMA["g(k2+2) = ∂f/∂γ"]
        G_TETA["g(k2+3) = ∂f/∂θ"]
    end
    
    GXCAR --> CHAIN
    DV1BETA --> CHAIN
    DV1GAMA --> CHAIN
    DV1TETA --> CHAIN
    CHAIN --> G_BETA
    CHAIN --> G_GAMA
    CHAIN --> G_TETA
```

The rotation matrix derivatives are computed analytically in [src/computeg.f90:162-204]() using trigonometric identities:

```
dv1beta(1) = -cos(β)*sin(γ)*cos(θ) - sin(β)*cos(γ)
dv2beta(1) = -sin(β)*sin(γ)*cos(θ) + cos(β)*cos(γ)
dv3beta(1) = 0
... (27 components total for 3 angles × 3 vectors × 3 dimensions)
```

For each atom, the contribution to the angle gradient is ([src/computeg.f90:217-234]()):

```
for k = 1 to 3:
  g(k2+1) += (coor(idatom,1)*dv1beta(k) + 
              coor(idatom,2)*dv2beta(k) + 
              coor(idatom,3)*dv3beta(k)) * gxcar(icart, k)
```

This efficiently computes how changes in rotation angles affect the objective function through all atoms in the molecule.

**Sources:** [src/computeg.f90:145-241]()

## Distance Gradient Function (gparc)

The `gparc` subroutine in [src/gparc.f90:9-86]() computes the gradient of distance penalties. For each atom pair where `datom < tol`:

```
dtemp = fscale(i) * fscale(j) * 4 * (datom - tol)

gxcar(icart, k) += dtemp * vdiff(k)
gxcar(jcart, k) -= dtemp * vdiff(k)
```

This implements the derivative of the quadratic penalty:

```
∂/∂x [(d² - tol)²] = 4(d² - tol) · ∂d²/∂x = 4(d² - tol) · 2(x_i - x_j)
```

The gradient contributions are equal and opposite for the two atoms, reflecting Newton's third law.

For short radius penalties ([src/gparc.f90:65-81]()):

```
if datom < short_tol:
  short_tol_scale = sqrt(short_radius_scale(i) * short_radius_scale(j)) * (tol²/short_tol²)
  dtemp = fscale(i) * fscale(j) * 4 * short_tol_scale * (datom - short_tol)
  
  gxcar(icart, k) += dtemp * vdiff(k)
  gxcar(jcart, k) -= dtemp * vdiff(k)
```

**Sources:** [src/gparc.f90:9-86]()

## Constraint Gradient Function (gwalls)

The `gwalls` subroutine in [src/gwalls.f90:9-327]() computes gradients for geometric constraints. Each constraint type has its own analytical gradient formula.

### Example: Inside Cube Constraint

For `ityperest = 2` (inside cube), [src/gwalls.f90:24-43]():

```
if x < xmin:
  gxcar(icart, 1) += scale * 2 * (x - xmin)
  
if x > xmax:
  gxcar(icart, 1) += scale * 2 * (x - xmax)
```

This is the derivative of the penalty `scale * (x - xmin)²` or `scale * (x - xmax)²`.

### Example: Outside Sphere Constraint

For `ityperest = 4` (outside sphere), [src/gwalls.f90:63-75]():

```
d = (x - x₀)² + (y - y₀)² + (z - z₀)² - r²

if d > 0:
  gxcar(icart, 1) += 4 * scale2 * (x - x₀) * d
  gxcar(icart, 2) += 4 * scale2 * (y - y₀) * d
  gxcar(icart, 3) += 4 * scale2 * (z - z₀) * d
```

This is the derivative of `scale2 * d²` using the chain rule.

### Example: Cylinder Constraint

For `ityperest = 12` (inside cylinder), the gradient is more complex ([src/gwalls.f90:202-242]()). It decomposes the violation into:
- Axial distance from cylinder base: controlled by `w`
- Radial distance from cylinder axis: controlled by `d`

The gradient combines contributions from both components using the chain rule.

**Sources:** [src/gwalls.f90:9-327]()

## Variable Indexing Scheme

The optimization variables `x` are organized as follows:

| Range | Content | Formula |
|-------|---------|---------|
| `1 : 3*ntotmol` | Center-of-mass coordinates | `x(3*(imol-1) + k)` for molecule `imol`, coordinate `k ∈ {1,2,3}` |
| `3*ntotmol+1 : 6*ntotmol` | Euler angles | `x(3*ntotmol + 3*(imol-1) + j)` for molecule `imol`, angle `j ∈ {1,2,3}` |

The indexing variables used in the code:

```
ilubar = 3 * (imol - 1)              ! Index into center-of-mass section
ilugan = 3*ntotmol + 3*(imol - 1)    ! Index into angle section
k1 = ilubar                          ! For gradient accumulation
k2 = ilugan                          ! For gradient accumulation
```

The correspondence between atoms and molecules is maintained through:

```
icart        ! Global atom index (1 to ntotal)
ibtype(icart) ! Molecule type of atom icart
ibmol(icart)  ! Molecule instance number within type
```

**Sources:** [src/computef.f90:40-109](), [src/computeg.f90:43-96](), [src/computeg.f90:148-241]()

## Performance Characteristics

The objective function evaluation scales as:

| Operation | Complexity | Notes |
|-----------|-----------|-------|
| Coordinate transformation | O(N) | Loop over all atoms |
| Constraint evaluation | O(N·C) | C = average constraints per atom (typically small) |
| Cell construction | O(N) | Insert each atom into cell list |
| Distance evaluation | O(N) | With cell indexing; O(N²) without |
| Gradient transformation | O(N) | Chain rule application |

The cell-based spatial indexing is critical: without it, the distance evaluation would require checking all O(N²) atom pairs. With cells, each atom only checks its 14 neighboring cells, reducing the expected complexity to O(N) for uniformly distributed atoms.

**Sources:** [src/computef.f90](), [src/computeg.f90](), [src/fparc.f90](), [src/gparc.f90]()

## Key Data Structures

The following arrays are used during objective function evaluation:

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Input Variables"
        X["x(1:n)<br/>Generalized coordinates<br/>xcm + angles"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Cartesian Representation"
        XCART["xcart(ntotal, 3)<br/>Cartesian coordinates<br/>of all atoms"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Spatial Index"
        LATOMFIRST["latomfirst(ncells(1:3))<br/>First atom in each cell"]
        LATOMNEXT["latomnext(ntotal)<br/>Next atom in same cell"]
        LCELLFIRST["lcellfirst<br/>First occupied cell"]
        LCELLNEXT["lcellnext(ncells_total)<br/>Next occupied cell"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Atom Properties"
        RADIUS["radius(ntotal)<br/>Effective radius"]
        FSCALE["fscale(ntotal)<br/>Penalty scale factor"]
        FIXEDATOM["fixedatom(ntotal)<br/>Is atom fixed?"]
        IBTYPE["ibtype(ntotal)<br/>Molecule type"]
        IBMOL["ibmol(ntotal)<br/>Molecule number"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Constraint Data"
        NRATOM["nratom(ntotal)<br/>Number of constraints<br/>per atom"]
        IRATOM["iratom(ntotal, maxrest)<br/>Constraint indices"]
        RESTPARS["restpars(nrest, maxpar)<br/>Constraint parameters"]
        ITYPEREST["ityperest(nrest)<br/>Constraint type"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Gradients"
        GXCAR["gxcar(ntotal, 3)<br/>Cartesian gradients<br/>∂f/∂xcart"]
        G["g(1:n)<br/>Generalized gradients<br/>∂f/∂x"]
    end
    
    X --> XCART
    XCART --> LATOMFIRST
    XCART --> LATOMNEXT
    LATOMFIRST --> LCELLFIRST
    LATOMNEXT --> LCELLNEXT
    
    XCART --> GXCAR
    GXCAR --> G
    
    RADIUS --> FPARC["fparc, gparc"]
    FSCALE --> FPARC
    FIXEDATOM --> FPARC
    IBTYPE --> FPARC
    IBMOL --> FPARC
    
    NRATOM --> COMPREST["comprest, gwalls"]
    IRATOM --> COMPREST
    RESTPARS --> COMPREST
    ITYPEREST --> COMPREST
```

**Sources:** [src/compute_data.f90](), [src/sizes.f90]()

# Page: Atom-to-Atom Interactions

# Atom-to-Atom Interactions

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [src/computef.f90](src/computef.f90)
- [src/computeg.f90](src/computeg.f90)
- [src/fparc.f90](src/fparc.f90)
- [src/gparc.f90](src/gparc.f90)

</details>



## Purpose and Scope

This document describes the pairwise atom-to-atom interaction calculations that form the distance penalty component of Packmol's objective function. These calculations ensure that molecules maintain appropriate separation distances during the packing optimization process.

For the overall objective function structure (including constraint penalties), see [Objective Function Evaluation](#4.6). For the spatial acceleration structures that make these calculations efficient, see [Spatial Management System](#4.5). For how coordinates are transformed before distance calculations, see [Coordinate Transformations](#4.8).

## System Overview

The atom-to-atom interaction system computes quadratic penalties when pairs of atoms are closer than their combined tolerance radii. These penalties drive the optimization process to find configurations where all atoms are properly separated while satisfying geometric constraints.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Objective Function Evaluation"
        COMPUTEF["computef.f90<br/>Main function evaluator"]
        COMPUTEG["computeg.f90<br/>Main gradient evaluator"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Coordinate Processing"
        XCART["xcart array<br/>Cartesian coordinates"]
        CELL_SETUP["Cell indexing setup<br/>latomfirst, latomnext"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Pairwise Calculations"
        FPARC["fparc.f90<br/>Distance penalty function"]
        GPARC["gparc.f90<br/>Gradient subroutine"]
        DELTA["delta_vector<br/>PBC-aware distance"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Radius System"
        RADIUS["radius array<br/>Current tolerance"]
        RADIUS_INI["radius_ini array<br/>Target distance"]
        SHORT_RADIUS["short_radius array<br/>Close contact penalty"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Output"
        F["f<br/>Total objective value"]
        FDIST["fdist<br/>Max overlap depth"]
        G["g array<br/>Gradient vector"]
        GXCAR["gxcar array<br/>Cartesian gradient"]
    end
    
    COMPUTEF --> XCART
    XCART --> CELL_SETUP
    CELL_SETUP --> FPARC
    FPARC --> DELTA
    FPARC --> RADIUS
    FPARC --> RADIUS_INI
    FPARC --> SHORT_RADIUS
    FPARC --> F
    FPARC --> FDIST
    
    COMPUTEG --> XCART
    COMPUTEG --> GPARC
    GPARC --> DELTA
    GPARC --> RADIUS
    GPARC --> SHORT_RADIUS
    GPARC --> GXCAR
    GXCAR --> G
    
    style FPARC fill:#ffcccc
    style GPARC fill:#ccffcc
    style DELTA fill:#ccccff
```

**Sources:** [src/computef.f90:1-155](), [src/computeg.f90:1-246](), [src/fparc.f90:1-79](), [src/gparc.f90:1-88]()

## Distance Penalty Function

The function `fparc` in [src/fparc.f90]() computes the penalty for a single atom's interactions with all atoms in a given linked list. The penalty is applied when the squared distance between atoms falls below their combined tolerance radii.

### Basic Penalty Formula

For each atom pair (i, j), the penalty is computed as:

```
tol = (radius[i] + radius[j])²
if (datom < tol):
    penalty = fscale[i] × fscale[j] × (datom - tol)²
```

Where:
- `datom` is the squared distance between atoms
- `tol` is the squared sum of tolerance radii
- `fscale` is a per-atom scaling factor

The function iterates through atom pairs using the linked-list structure, skipping pairs that should not be evaluated:

| Skip Condition | Reason |
|----------------|--------|
| `ibtype(jcart)` not in `comptype` | Molecule type not being optimized |
| `ibmol(icart) == ibmol(jcart)` and same type | Atoms from same molecule |
| Both `fixedatom(icart)` and `fixedatom(jcart)` | Both atoms fixed |

**Sources:** [src/fparc.f90:10-77]()

### Distance Tracking

Beyond computing penalties, `fparc` also tracks the maximum overlap depth using `radius_ini`, which represents the target minimum distance:

```fortran
tol = (radius_ini(icart)+radius_ini(jcart))**2
fdist = dmax1(tol-datom,fdist)
```

This `fdist` value provides a measure of how far the current configuration is from achieving all target distances, independent of the penalty function.

**Sources:** [src/fparc.f90:68-73]()

## Gradient Computation

The `gparc` subroutine in [src/gparc.f90]() computes the gradient of the distance penalty with respect to Cartesian coordinates. This gradient is essential for the GENCAN optimizer to determine descent directions.

### Gradient Formula

For a pair of atoms within the tolerance distance:

```
dtemp = fscale[i] × fscale[j] × 4 × (datom - tol)
∇penalty[i] = dtemp × (x[i] - x[j])
∇penalty[j] = -dtemp × (x[i] - x[j])
```

The factor of 4 comes from the chain rule derivative of `(datom - tol)²` where `datom = ||x[i] - x[j]||²`.

The gradient is accumulated into the `gxcar` array, which stores gradients in Cartesian space before they are transformed back to generalized coordinates (center-of-mass + Euler angles) by `computeg`.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    ATOM_PAIR["Atom pair (i,j)"] --> CHECK_DISTANCE["Check if datom < tol"]
    CHECK_DISTANCE -->|Yes| COMPUTE_VDIFF["vdiff = delta_vector(xi, xj)"]
    COMPUTE_VDIFF --> COMPUTE_DTEMP["dtemp = 4×fscale[i]×fscale[j]×(datom-tol)"]
    COMPUTE_DTEMP --> UPDATE_GRAD["gxcar[i,:] += dtemp×vdiff<br/>gxcar[j,:] -= dtemp×vdiff"]
    UPDATE_GRAD --> CHECK_SHORT["Check short radius"]
    CHECK_SHORT -->|Active| SHORT_GRAD["Add short radius gradient"]
    CHECK_SHORT -->|Inactive| NEXT
    SHORT_GRAD --> NEXT["Next atom pair"]
    CHECK_DISTANCE -->|No| NEXT
```

**Sources:** [src/gparc.f90:9-86]()

## Radius Types and Tolerance System

Packmol uses three distinct radius types for each atom, stored in separate arrays. Understanding their roles is critical to understanding the penalty system.

| Array Name | Type | Purpose | Usage |
|------------|------|---------|-------|
| `radius` | Dynamic | Current tolerance for penalty calculation | Penalty applied when `datom < (radius[i]+radius[j])²` |
| `radius_ini` | Static | Target minimum distance | Used to track overlap depth in `fdist` |
| `short_radius` | Static | Close contact threshold | Triggers additional steep penalty |
| `short_radius_scale` | Static | Penalty scaling factor | Multiplies short radius penalty |

### Dynamic Radius Adjustment

The `radius` array can be dynamically adjusted during optimization (controlled by the `discale` parameter in input), allowing the tolerance to change over time. This enables a strategy where molecules initially pack with tighter constraints that gradually relax.

**Sources:** [src/fparc.f90:22-23,51-68](), [src/gparc.f90:21-22,51-82]()

## Short Radius Penalty System

The short radius system provides an additional steep penalty when atoms get extremely close, helping prevent molecular overlap and improving convergence.

### Two-Level Penalty Structure

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Distance Ranges"
        FAR["datom > (radius[i]+radius[j])²<br/>No penalty"]
        MEDIUM["(short_radius[i]+short_radius[j])² < datom < (radius[i]+radius[j])²<br/>Standard penalty only"]
        CLOSE["datom < (short_radius[i]+short_radius[j])²<br/>Standard + Short penalty"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Penalty Contributions"
        STD_PENALTY["Standard Penalty:<br/>fscale[i]×fscale[j]×(datom-tol)²"]
        SHORT_PENALTY["Short Penalty:<br/>fscale[i]×fscale[j]×scale×(datom-short_tol)²"]
    end
    
    CLOSE --> STD_PENALTY
    CLOSE --> SHORT_PENALTY
    MEDIUM --> STD_PENALTY
```

### Short Radius Calculation Details

When both atoms have short radii enabled (`use_short_radius` flag):

```fortran
short_tol = (short_radius(icart)+short_radius(jcart))**2
if ( datom < short_tol ) then
    short_tol_penalty = datom-short_tol
    short_tol_scale = dsqrt(short_radius_scale(icart)*short_radius_scale(jcart))
    short_tol_scale = short_tol_scale*(tol**2/short_tol**2)
    penalty = penalty + fscale(icart)*fscale(jcart)*short_tol_scale*short_tol_penalty**2
end if
```

The scaling factor `short_tol_scale` is computed as the geometric mean of the two atoms' scale factors, multiplied by a ratio that accounts for the difference in tolerance magnitudes. This ensures the short radius penalty has appropriate relative magnitude.

**Sources:** [src/fparc.f90:58-66](), [src/gparc.f90:65-81]()

## Spatial Optimization via Cell Indexing

The naive approach of computing all pairwise distances would require O(N²) operations for N atoms. Packmol reduces this to O(N) using spatial cell indexing.

### Neighbor Search Integration

In `computef` and `computeg`, the pairwise calculations are organized to examine only nearby cells:

```mermaid
graph TB
    OCCUPIED_CELLS["Iterate occupied cells<br/>via lcellfirst/lcellnext"] --> ATOMS_IN_CELL["Iterate atoms in cell<br/>via latomfirst/latomnext"]
    ATOMS_IN_CELL --> INTERACTIONS["Compute interactions with<br/>14 neighboring cells"]
    
    subgraph "14 Neighbor Cells"
        SELF["Same cell<br/>latomnext(icart)"]
        FACES["3 face neighbors<br/>(+1,0,0), (0,+1,0), (0,0,+1)"]
        EDGES["6 edge neighbors<br/>e.g. (+1,+1,0), (+1,0,+1)"]
        VERTICES["4 vertex neighbors<br/>e.g. (+1,+1,+1), (+1,+1,-1)"]
    end
    
    INTERACTIONS --> SELF
    INTERACTIONS --> FACES
    INTERACTIONS --> EDGES
    INTERACTIONS --> VERTICES
    SELF --> FPARC["fparc(icart, jcart_list)"]
    FACES --> FPARC
    EDGES --> FPARC
    VERTICES --> FPARC
```

The cell size is chosen such that only adjacent cells need to be checked. The use of periodic boundary conditions via `cell_ind` function wraps cell indices appropriately.

**Sources:** [src/computef.f90:115-151](), [src/computeg.f90:105-141]()

## Neighbor Search Pattern

The neighbor search examines 14 cells: the current cell plus 13 forward neighbors in a 3D stencil. This avoids double-counting pairs while ensuring all pairs within cutoff distance are evaluated.

### Cell Pattern in computef

The calls to `fparc` from `computef` follow this pattern:

| Cell Offset | Description | Code Line |
|-------------|-------------|-----------|
| (0,0,0) | Self-cell interactions | [src/computef.f90:128]() |
| (+1,0,0) | Face neighbor | [src/computef.f90:130]() |
| (0,+1,0) | Face neighbor | [src/computef.f90:131]() |
| (0,0,+1) | Face neighbor | [src/computef.f90:132]() |
| (+1,-1,0) | Edge neighbor | [src/computef.f90:134]() |
| (+1,0,-1) | Edge neighbor | [src/computef.f90:135]() |
| (0,+1,-1) | Edge neighbor | [src/computef.f90:136]() |
| (0,+1,+1) | Edge neighbor | [src/computef.f90:137]() |
| (+1,+1,0) | Edge neighbor | [src/computef.f90:138]() |
| (+1,0,+1) | Edge neighbor | [src/computef.f90:139]() |
| (+1,-1,-1) | Vertex neighbor | [src/computef.f90:141]() |
| (+1,-1,+1) | Vertex neighbor | [src/computef.f90:142]() |
| (+1,+1,-1) | Vertex neighbor | [src/computef.f90:143]() |
| (+1,+1,+1) | Vertex neighbor | [src/computef.f90:144]() |

### Cell Pattern Differences

Note that `computeg` uses a slightly different pattern (13 neighbors instead of 14 in one dimension), but the logic is equivalent - both ensure all pairs are evaluated exactly once:

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "computef pattern"
        CF_SELF["Self cell"]
        CF_FORWARD["13 forward neighbors<br/>with negative offsets"]
    end
    
    subgraph "computeg pattern"
        CG_SELF["Self cell"]
        CG_FORWARD["13 forward neighbors<br/>different arrangement"]
    end
    
    CF_SELF -.equivalent.-> CG_SELF
    CF_FORWARD -.equivalent.-> CG_FORWARD
```

Both patterns examine the same set of atom pairs but with different cell iteration orders.

**Sources:** [src/computef.f90:128-144](), [src/computeg.f90:118-134]()

## Periodic Boundary Conditions

All distance calculations use the `delta_vector` function from the PBC module, which computes the minimum image distance when periodic boundary conditions are active:

```fortran
vdiff = delta_vector(xcart(icart,:), xcart(jcart,:), pbc_length)
datom = (vdiff(1))**2 + (vdiff(2))**2 + (vdiff(3))**2
```

This ensures that:
1. In non-periodic systems, `delta_vector` simply returns the direct difference
2. In periodic systems, it returns the shortest vector considering periodic images
3. The same code path handles both cases transparently

**Sources:** [src/fparc.f90:53-54](), [src/gparc.f90:52-53]()

## Performance Characteristics

The atom-to-atom interaction calculation dominates computational cost in Packmol. Key performance characteristics:

| Aspect | Complexity | Notes |
|--------|-----------|-------|
| Naive pairwise | O(N²) | Would be prohibitively expensive |
| With cell indexing | O(N) | Assuming uniform density |
| Cell size | Set by max radius | Determines neighbors to check |
| Gradient computation | O(N) | Same as function evaluation |
| PBC overhead | O(1) per pair | Minimal cost for distance wrapping |

The efficiency of this system enables Packmol to handle systems with millions of atoms in reasonable time.

**Sources:** [src/fparc.f90:10-77](), [src/gparc.f90:9-86]()

---

# Page: Coordinate Transformations

# Coordinate Transformations

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [src/computef.f90](src/computef.f90)
- [src/computeg.f90](src/computeg.f90)
- [src/initial.f90](src/initial.f90)

</details>



## Purpose and Scope

This page documents Packmol's coordinate transformation system, which converts between three representations: generalized coordinates (center of mass + Euler angles), reference coordinates (molecular templates), and Cartesian coordinates (3D atom positions). These transformations are fundamental to the optimization process and appear in every function and gradient evaluation.

For information about how these coordinates are used in the optimization loop, see [Optimization Engine (GENCAN)](#4.4). For details on how Cartesian coordinates are used in spatial queries, see [Spatial Management System](#4.5).

---

## Overview of Coordinate Representations

Packmol maintains three distinct coordinate representations to enable efficient optimization of molecular packing:

```mermaid
graph TB
    GEN["Generalized Coordinates<br/>(x array)<br/>Position: xcm[3]<br/>Orientation: beta, gamma, theta"]
    REF["Reference Coordinates<br/>(coor array)<br/>Molecular template<br/>Atom positions relative to CM"]
    CART["Cartesian Coordinates<br/>(xcart array)<br/>Final 3D positions<br/>All atoms in space"]
    
    GEN -->|"eulerrmat<br/>compcart"| CART
    REF -->|"compcart"| CART
    
    CART -->|"Chain rule<br/>dv1beta, dv2beta, etc."| GRAD["Gradient in<br/>Generalized Space<br/>(g array)"]
    
    style GEN fill:#f9f9f9
    style REF fill:#f9f9f9
    style CART fill:#f9f9f9
    style GRAD fill:#f9f9f9
```

**Sources:** [src/computef.f90:38-72](), [src/computeg.f90:39-66](), [src/initial.f90:121-138]()

---

## Generalized Coordinates (x array)

The optimization variables are stored in the `x(n)` array using a two-block structure:

| Block | Range | Content | Description |
|-------|-------|---------|-------------|
| Position | `1` to `ntotmol*3` | `xcm[1:3]` for each molecule | Center of mass coordinates (x, y, z) |
| Orientation | `ntotmol*3+1` to `n` | `beta, gamma, theta` for each molecule | Euler angles defining rotation |

The array is accessed using index variables `ilubar` (position block) and `ilugan` (angle block):

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "x array structure"
        POS["Position Block<br/>ilubar indices<br/>Molecule 1: x[1:3]<br/>Molecule 2: x[4:6]<br/>...<br/>Molecule N: x[3N-2:3N]"]
        ANG["Angle Block<br/>ilugan indices<br/>Molecule 1: x[3N+1:3N+3]<br/>Molecule 2: x[3N+4:3N+6]<br/>...<br/>Molecule N: x[6N-2:6N]"]
    end
    
    POS --> ITER1["ilubar += 3<br/>per molecule"]
    ANG --> ITER2["ilugan += 3<br/>per molecule"]
    
    style POS fill:#f9f9f9
    style ANG fill:#f9f9f9
```

### Position Block Layout

For a system with `ntype` molecule types, each containing `nmols(itype)` molecules:

```fortran
ilubar = 0
do itype = 1, ntype
  do imol = 1, nmols(itype)
    xcm(1:3) = x(ilubar+1:ilubar+3)  ! Center of mass
    ilubar = ilubar + 3
  end do
end do
```

**Sources:** [src/computef.f90:40-52](), [src/initial.f90:89-116]()

### Angle Block Layout

The Euler angles follow the same molecule ordering as positions, starting at offset `ntotmol*3`:

```fortran
ilugan = ntotmol*3
do itype = 1, ntype
  do imol = 1, nmols(itype)
    beta  = x(ilugan+1)
    gamma = x(ilugan+2)
    theta = x(ilugan+3)
    ilugan = ilugan + 3
  end do
end do
```

Angles can be constrained to specific ranges using `constrain_rot(itype, axis)` and `rot_bound(itype, axis, 1:2)`. Unconstrained angles are initialized in the full range `[0, 2π]`.

**Sources:** [src/computef.f90:56-58](), [src/initial.f90:96-116](), [src/initial.f90:431-458]()

---

## Reference Coordinates (coor array)

The `coor` array stores template molecular structures with atom positions relative to the molecular center of mass:

| Array | Dimensions | Content |
|-------|------------|---------|
| `coor(idatom, 1:3)` | `maxatom × 3` | Reference (x, y, z) for each atom |
| `idfirst(itype)` | `ntype` | Index of first atom for molecule type |
| `natoms(itype)` | `ntype` | Number of atoms per molecule type |

Atoms are accessed using an offset pattern:

```fortran
idatom = idfirst(itype) - 1
do iatom = 1, natoms(itype)
  idatom = idatom + 1
  ! coor(idatom, 1:3) contains reference coordinates
end do
```

These reference coordinates are read from PDB or XYZ files during input parsing and remain constant throughout optimization. They define the rigid molecular geometry.

**Sources:** [src/computef.f90:64-68](), [src/computeg.f90:61-65](), [src/initial.f90:56-70]()

---

## Cartesian Coordinates (xcart array)

The `xcart(icart, 1:3)` array stores the actual 3D positions of all atoms in the system:

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "xcart array"
        MOV["Movable Atoms<br/>icart: 1 to ntotat-nfixedat<br/>Updated each iteration"]
        FIX["Fixed Atoms<br/>icart: ntotat-nfixedat+1 to ntotat<br/>Constant positions"]
    end
    
    MOV --> CELL["setcell()<br/>Assign to spatial cells"]
    MOV --> DIST["Distance calculations<br/>fparc, gparc"]
    MOV --> CONST["Constraint checks<br/>comprest, gwalls"]
    
    FIX --> FCELL["Fixed cell lists<br/>latomfix"]
    
    style MOV fill:#f9f9f9
    style FIX fill:#f9f9f9
```

The `icart` index increments linearly through all atoms:

```fortran
icart = 0
do itype = 1, ntype
  do imol = 1, nmols(itype)
    do iatom = 1, natoms(itype)
      icart = icart + 1
      ! xcart(icart, 1:3) contains Cartesian position
    end do
  end do
end do
```

Additional metadata arrays indexed by `icart`:
- `ibtype(icart)`: Molecule type index
- `ibmol(icart)`: Molecule number within type
- `fixedatom(icart)`: Boolean flag for fixed atoms
- `latomnext(icart)`: Linked list pointer for spatial indexing

**Sources:** [src/computef.f90:42-101](), [src/initial.f90:123-165]()

---

## Transformation: Generalized to Cartesian

### Step 1: Euler Rotation Matrix (eulerrmat)

The `eulerrmat` subroutine computes three basis vectors `v1`, `v2`, `v3` from Euler angles:

```mermaid
graph LR
    ANGLES["Euler Angles<br/>beta, gamma, theta"] --> TRIG["Trigonometric<br/>Functions<br/>cb, sb, cg, sg, ct, st"]
    TRIG --> V1["v1[3]<br/>First basis vector"]
    TRIG --> V2["v2[3]<br/>Second basis vector"]
    TRIG --> V3["v3[3]<br/>Third basis vector"]
    
    V1 --> ROT["Rotation Matrix<br/>[v1 | v2 | v3]"]
    V2 --> ROT
    V3 --> ROT
    
    style ANGLES fill:#f9f9f9
    style ROT fill:#f9f9f9
```

The rotation matrix columns are:

```
v1 = [ sb*sg*ct + cb*cg,   sb*cg*ct - cb*sg,   sb*st ]
v2 = [ cb*sg*ct - sb*cg,   cb*cg*ct + sb*sg,   cb*st ]
v3 = [      -sg*st,             cg*st,           ct   ]
```

Where: `cb = cos(beta)`, `sb = sin(beta)`, `cg = cos(gamma)`, `sg = sin(gamma)`, `ct = cos(theta)`, `st = sin(theta)`

**Sources:** [src/computef.f90:60](), [src/computeg.f90:60](), [src/initial.f90:130]()

### Step 2: Cartesian Composition (compcart)

The `compcart` subroutine applies the rotation matrix and translation:

```mermaid
graph LR
    XCM["Center of Mass<br/>xcm[3]"] --> ADD["Vector Addition"]
    COOR["Reference Position<br/>coor[idatom, 1:3]"] --> ROT["Matrix-Vector<br/>Multiplication<br/>v1, v2, v3"]
    ROT --> ADD
    ADD --> XCART["Cartesian Position<br/>xcart[icart, 1:3]"]
    
    style XCM fill:#f9f9f9
    style COOR fill:#f9f9f9
    style XCART fill:#f9f9f9
```

The mathematical formula:

```
xcart[icart, :] = xcm[:] + coor[idatom, 1] * v1[:] 
                         + coor[idatom, 2] * v2[:] 
                         + coor[idatom, 3] * v3[:]
```

This transformation appears in three key locations:

1. **Initial point generation:** [src/initial.f90:126-138]()
2. **Function evaluation:** [src/computef.f90:52-72]()
3. **Gradient evaluation:** [src/computeg.f90:54-66]()

**Sources:** [src/computef.f90:72](), [src/computeg.f90:66](), [src/initial.f90:135]()

---

## Full Transformation Pipeline

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    START["Start with x array"] --> EXTRACT["Extract for molecule imol:<br/>xcm = x[ilubar+1:ilubar+3]<br/>beta = x[ilugan+1]<br/>gamma = x[ilugan+2]<br/>theta = x[ilugan+3]"]
    
    EXTRACT --> EULER["call eulerrmat(beta, gamma, theta, v1, v2, v3)"]
    
    EULER --> LOOP["Loop over atoms:<br/>do iatom = 1, natoms(itype)"]
    
    LOOP --> COMP["call compcart(<br/>  xcart[icart,1:3],<br/>  xcm,<br/>  coor[idatom,1:3],<br/>  v1, v2, v3)"]
    
    COMP --> STORE["xcart[icart,:] now contains<br/>3D Cartesian position"]
    
    STORE --> MORE{"More<br/>atoms?"}
    MORE -->|Yes| INCR["icart += 1<br/>idatom += 1"]
    INCR --> LOOP
    MORE -->|No| NEXT["ilubar += 3<br/>ilugan += 3<br/>Next molecule"]
    
    style START fill:#f9f9f9
    style EULER fill:#e8f4f8
    style COMP fill:#e8f4f8
    style STORE fill:#f9f9f9
```

**Sources:** [src/computef.f90:40-108](), [src/computeg.f90:43-96]()

---

## Gradient Transformation via Chain Rule

Computing gradients requires the reverse transformation: from Cartesian gradient `gxcar(icart, k)` to generalized gradient `g(n)`.

### Cartesian Gradient Accumulation

During function evaluation, gradients are accumulated in `gxcar`:

```fortran
gxcar(icart, 1:3) = 0.d0  ! Reset
! Distance penalties contribute via gparc
! Constraint penalties contribute via gwalls
```

**Sources:** [src/computeg.f90:33](), [src/computeg.f90:69-71](), [src/computeg.f90:99-143]()

### Position Gradient (Direct)

The gradient with respect to center of mass is straightforward:

```fortran
do k = 1, 3
  g(k1+k) = g(k1+k) + gxcar(icart, k)
end do
```

This is a direct copy because `∂xcart/∂xcm = I` (identity matrix).

**Sources:** [src/computeg.f90:212-214]()

### Angle Gradient (Chain Rule)

The gradient with respect to Euler angles requires the chain rule:

```
g(k2+1) += Σ_k [∂xcart_k/∂beta  * gxcar(icart, k)]
g(k2+2) += Σ_k [∂xcart_k/∂gamma * gxcar(icart, k)]
g(k2+3) += Σ_k [∂xcart_k/∂theta * gxcar(icart, k)]
```

The partial derivatives are:

```
∂xcart_k/∂beta  = coor[idatom,1] * dv1beta[k]  + coor[idatom,2] * dv2beta[k]  + coor[idatom,3] * dv3beta[k]
∂xcart_k/∂gamma = coor[idatom,1] * dv1gamma[k] + coor[idatom,2] * dv2gamma[k] + coor[idatom,3] * dv3gamma[k]
∂xcart_k/∂theta = coor[idatom,1] * dv1theta[k] + coor[idatom,2] * dv2theta[k] + coor[idatom,3] * dv3theta[k]
```

**Sources:** [src/computeg.f90:217-234]()

### Rotation Matrix Derivatives

The `dv*` arrays contain derivatives of the rotation matrix basis vectors:

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Derivative Arrays"
        DVB["dv1beta, dv2beta, dv3beta<br/>∂[v1,v2,v3]/∂beta"]
        DVG["dv1gamma, dv2gamma, dv3gamma<br/>∂[v1,v2,v3]/∂gamma"]
        DVT["dv1theta, dv2theta, dv3theta<br/>∂[v1,v2,v3]/∂theta"]
    end
    
    TRIG["Trigonometric<br/>cb, sb, cg, sg, ct, st"] --> DVB
    TRIG --> DVG
    TRIG --> DVT
    
    DVB --> CHAIN["Chain Rule<br/>Multiplication"]
    DVG --> CHAIN
    DVT --> CHAIN
    
    COOR["coor[idatom,1:3]"] --> CHAIN
    GXCAR["gxcar[icart,k]"] --> CHAIN
    
    CHAIN --> GRAD["g[k2+1:k2+3]"]
    
    style DVB fill:#f9f9f9
    style DVG fill:#f9f9f9
    style DVT fill:#f9f9f9
```

Example derivatives for `dv1beta`:

```fortran
dv1beta(1) = - cb * sg * ct - sb * cg
dv1beta(2) = - cb * cg * ct + sb * sg
dv1beta(3) =   cb * st
```

All 27 derivatives (9 per angle) are computed from trigonometric functions in [src/computeg.f90:162-204]().

**Sources:** [src/computeg.f90:158-204](), [src/computeg.f90:217-234]()

---

## Index Management Pattern

The transformation code follows a consistent index management pattern across all three arrays:

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "Index Variables"
        K1["k1, k2<br/>Generalized gradient<br/>Position and angle offsets"]
        ILUBAR["ilubar, ilugan<br/>Generalized coordinates<br/>Position and angle offsets"]
        ICART["icart<br/>Cartesian coordinates<br/>Linear atom index"]
        IDATOM["idatom<br/>Reference coordinates<br/>Template atom index"]
    end
    
    K1 --> GARRAY["g array"]
    ILUBAR --> XARRAY["x array"]
    ICART --> XCARR["xcart array"]
    IDATOM --> COORR["coor array"]
    
    style K1 fill:#f9f9f9
    style ILUBAR fill:#f9f9f9
    style ICART fill:#f9f9f9
    style IDATOM fill:#f9f9f9
```

Typical loop structure:

```fortran
k1 = 0              ! Position gradient offset
k2 = ntotmol * 3    ! Angle gradient offset
ilubar = 0          ! Position variable offset
ilugan = ntotmol*3  ! Angle variable offset
icart = 0           ! Cartesian atom index

do itype = 1, ntype
  idatom = idfirst(itype) - 1  ! Reference offset
  
  do imol = 1, nmols(itype)
    ! Use ilubar, ilugan for x array access
    ! Use icart for xcart array access
    ! Use idatom for coor array access
    
    do iatom = 1, natoms(itype)
      icart = icart + 1
      idatom = idatom + 1
      ! Process atom
    end do
    
    ilubar = ilubar + 3
    ilugan = ilugan + 3
    k1 = k1 + 3
    k2 = k2 + 3
  end do
end do
```

**Sources:** [src/computeg.f90:147-241](), [src/computef.f90:40-108]()

---

## Type Masking with comptype

The `comptype(itype)` boolean array controls which molecule types are included in transformations:

| Mode | `comptype` State | Purpose |
|------|------------------|---------|
| Full optimization | All `.true.` | All molecules optimized together |
| Type-specific (via `swaptype`) | One type `.true.`, rest `.false.` | Isolate single molecule type |
| Initialization | Per-phase | Sequential constraint satisfaction |

This masking appears in loops:

```fortran
if(.not.comptype(itype)) then
  icart = icart + nmols(itype)*natoms(itype)
  cycle
end if
```

When a type is masked, its atoms are skipped but `icart` still increments to maintain consistent indexing.

**Sources:** [src/computef.f90:45-48](), [src/computeg.f90:49-52](), [src/initial.f90:44-45]()

---

## Performance Considerations

The coordinate transformation is performed in every function and gradient evaluation, making it performance-critical:

1. **Function evaluations:** Transform all atoms to compute distances and constraints
2. **Gradient evaluations:** Transform all atoms, then apply chain rule for all atoms
3. **Typical call frequency:** Hundreds to thousands of times per optimization

Key optimizations:
- In-place updates of `xcart` array
- Reuse of trigonometric values (`cb`, `sb`, etc.)
- Cell indexing built during transformation to avoid separate pass
- Skipping masked types via `comptype`

The transformation cost is O(ntotat) where `ntotat` is the total number of atoms. This is acceptable since subsequent distance calculations are O(ntotat) using cell indexing (see [Spatial Management System](#4.5)).

**Sources:** [src/computef.f90:1-154](), [src/computeg.f90:1-244]()

---

## Purpose and Scope

This document provides an overview of Packmol's comprehensive testing infrastructure, which validates both the correctness of molecular packing results and the robustness of the software interface. The testing system employs a multi-layered validation strategy combining Julia-based physical validation, shell-based interface testing, and continuous integration orchestration.

For detailed information about specific test components, see:
- Julia-based minimum distance validation: [5.1](#5.1)
- Shell-based interface and error handling tests: [5.2](#5.2)
- CI/CD pipeline configuration: [5.3](#5.3)

## Testing Architecture Overview

Packmol's testing system is organized as a hierarchical test orchestration framework with three primary validation layers:

```mermaid

        CI["GitHub Actions<br/>.github/workflows/actions.yml"]

        CHECK_MIND["check_mind()<br/>Distance Validator"]
        PDBTOOLS["PDBTools.jl<br/>PDB Parser"]
        CELLLIST["CellListMap.jl<br/>Distance Calculator"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Interface Validation Layer"
        TEST_CLI["test_cli.sh<br/>CLI Consistency Tests"]
        TEST_FAILED["test_failed.sh<br/>Error Handling Tests"]
        TEST_CONNECT["test_connectivity.sh<br/>Connectivity Tests"]
    end
```

## Test Categories and Input Files

The test suite includes 17+ input files organized into functional categories:

| Category | Input Files | Purpose |
|----------|-------------|---------|
| **Basic Functionality** | `water_box.inp`<br/>`mixture.inp`<br/>`ieee_signaling.inp` | Validate core packing without PBC or special constraints |
| **Fixed Molecules** | `toy_with_fixed.inp`<br/>`only_one_fixed.inp` | Test molecules with `fixed` keyword holding positions constant |
| **Spatial Constraints** | `spherical.inp`<br/>`bilayer.inp`<br/>`solvprotein.inp` | Test geometric constraints (inside/outside regions) |
| **Periodic Boundaries** | `water_box_pbc.inp`<br/>`water_box_pbc2.inp`<br/>`water_box_pbc_negative_coordinates.inp`<br/>`water_box_pbc_slab.inp`<br/>`water_box_pbc_outside_box.inp` | Validate PBC with various coordinate configurations |
| **Complex PBC Systems** | `mixture_pbc.inp`<br/>`bilayer_pbc.inp`<br/>`solvprotein_pbc.inp`<br/>`spherical_pbc.inp` | Test PBC combined with constraints |
| **Error Handling** | `water_box_failed.inp`<br/>`protein_outside_pbc_error.inp` | Validate error detection and reporting |

Sources: [testing/test.sh:8-24](), [testing/input_files/water_box_pbc_outside_box.inp:1-20](), [testing/input_files/mixture_pbc.inp:1-22]()

**Distance Validation Algorithm**

The `check_mind()` function implements a sophisticated validation algorithm:

1. **Parse Input**: Extract `tolerance`, `output`, `pbc`, and `precision` keywords from input file [testing/runtests.jl:39-55]()
2. **Read Structure**: Parse generated PDB using PDBTools [testing/runtests.jl:59]()
3. **Build Cell System**: Create `ParticleSystem` with cutoff = `tolerance * 1.5` for efficient neighbor search [testing/runtests.jl:60-65]()
4. **Calculate Minimum Distance**: Use `map_pairwise()` with custom reducer to find minimum inter-molecular distance [testing/runtests.jl:66]()
5. **Validate Threshold**: Ensure `mind >= tolerance * (1 - precision)` [testing/runtests.jl:67-74]()

The `update_mind()` function ensures molecules are identified by residue number, skipping intra-molecular atom pairs [testing/runtests.jl:25-29]().

Sources: [testing/runtests.jl:34-78]()

## Minimum Distance Calculation Subsystem

The validation system leverages Julia's CellListMap package for O(N) complexity distance calculations:

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "MinimumDistance Type"
        MIND_STRUCT["struct MinimumDistance<br/>i: atom index<br/>j: atom index<br/>d: distance<br/>Lines 20-24"]
    end
    
    subgraph "CellListMap Integration"
        PARTICLE_SYS["ParticleSystem<br/>positions: from PDB<br/>unitcell: PBC box<br/>cutoff: tolerance*1.5<br/>output: MinimumDistance"]
        
        MAP_PAIRWISE["map_pairwise()<br/>Parallel cell-based search"]
        
        UPDATE_MIND_FUNC["update_mind(i,j,d2,pdb,md)<br/>Skip same residue<br/>Track minimum<br/>Lines 25-29"]
        
        REDUCER["reducer(md1,md2)<br/>Return minimum<br/>Line 30"]
        
        COPY_OUT["copy_output(md)<br/>Line 31"]
        RESET_OUT["reset_output()<br/>Initialize to +Inf<br/>Line 32"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Validation Logic"
        THRESHOLD["Threshold Check<br/>mind.d >= (1-precision)*tolerance<br/>Line 67"]
        ERROR_REPORT["Error Report<br/>Include atom indices<br/>VMD-compatible indices<br/>Lines 68-74"]
    end
    
    MIND_STRUCT --> PARTICLE_SYS
    PARTICLE_SYS --> MAP_PAIRWISE
    MAP_PAIRWISE --> UPDATE_MIND_FUNC
    UPDATE_MIND_FUNC --> REDUCER
    REDUCER --> MAP_PAIRWISE
    COPY_OUT --> MAP_PAIRWISE
    RESET_OUT --> MAP_PAIRWISE
    
    MAP_PAIRWISE --> THRESHOLD
    THRESHOLD -->|"Fail"| ERROR_REPORT
```

Sources: [testing/runtests.jl:20-32](), [testing/runtests.jl:60-74]()

## CLI Consistency Testing Mechanism

The `test_cli.sh` script validates that all three command-line interface methods produce identical output:

| Invocation Method | Command Syntax | Output File Source |
|-------------------|----------------|-------------------|
| **Standard Input** | `packmol < input.txt` | Specified in `output` keyword in input file |
| **Input Flag** | `packmol -i input.tmp` | Specified in `output` keyword in input file |
| **Input and Output Flags** | `packmol -i input.txt -o output.txt` | Overridden by `-o` flag |

**Test Procedure**:
1. Filter input files to exclude `*_error.inp` and `*_fail*.inp` patterns [testing/test_cli.sh:124]()
2. Patch input files: replace `seed -1` with `seed 1024` for reproducibility [testing/test_cli.sh:150]()
3. Create three variants with different output filenames [testing/test_cli.sh:152]()
4. Execute packmol using each invocation method [testing/test_cli.sh:178,193,204]()
5. Use GNU `diff` to compare output files byte-by-byte [testing/test_cli.sh:217-218]()
6. Verify zero byte difference (identical files) [testing/test_cli.sh:219]()

Sources: [testing/test_cli.sh:1-241]()

## Error Handling Test Pattern

The `test_failed.sh` script validates that Packmol correctly detects and reports specific error conditions:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant TEST as test.sh
    participant FAILED as test_failed.sh
    participant PACKMOL as packmol binary
    participant LOG as packmol.log
    
    TEST->>FAILED: Execute with input file and pattern
    Note over TEST,FAILED: test_failed.sh input.inp log "PATTERN"
    
    FAILED->>PACKMOL: Run with failing input
    PACKMOL->>LOG: Write error messages
    PACKMOL->>FAILED: Exit with error code
    
    FAILED->>LOG: grep for expected pattern
    alt Pattern Found
        LOG->>FAILED: Pattern match
        FAILED->>TEST: Return success (error properly detected)
    else Pattern Not Found
        LOG->>FAILED: No match
        FAILED->>TEST: Return failure (error not detected)
    end
```

**Test Cases**:
1. `water_box_failed.inp` → Expect "FORCED" in log [testing/test.sh:27]()
2. `protein_outside_pbc_error.inp` → Expect "outside" in log [testing/test.sh:28]()

Sources: [testing/test.sh:26-28]()

## Continuous Integration Configuration

The GitHub Actions workflow orchestrates testing across multiple platforms and compiler configurations:

| Matrix Dimension | Values | Purpose |
|------------------|--------|---------|
| **Operating System** | `ubuntu-latest`, `macOS-latest` | Cross-platform validation |
| **GCC Version** | `13` | Consistent compiler version |
| **Build System** | `make`, `cmake` | Validate both build systems |

**Pipeline Stages**:
1. **Checkout**: Retrieve code from repository [.github/workflows/actions.yml:20]()
2. **Setup Fortran**: Install GCC 13 using `fortran-lang/setup-fortran` [.github/workflows/actions.yml:21-25]()
3. **Compile (make)**: Run `./configure && make` [.github/workflows/actions.yml:27-32]()
4. **Compile (cmake)**: Run `cmake ./ && cmake --build ./` [.github/workflows/actions.yml:34-38]()
5. **Test**: Execute `install_julia.sh` followed by `test.sh` [.github/workflows/actions.yml:40-45]()

This creates 4 test jobs per push: (ubuntu×make, ubuntu×cmake, macOS×make, macOS×cmake), with failure isolation via `fail-fast: false` [.github/workflows/actions.yml:11]().

Sources: [.github/workflows/actions.yml:1-46]()

## Test Input File Requirements

For Julia validation tests to function correctly, PDB files must adhere to specific structural requirements:

**Structural Constraints**:
- Each molecule must be identified as a single residue [testing/runtests.jl:7-11]()
- Proteins must have one residue name for all atoms
- Residue numbers can be overwritten using the `resnumbers` option in input files
- The `update_mind()` function uses `residue(pdb[i]) == residue(pdb[j])` to skip intra-molecular pairs [testing/runtests.jl:26]()

**Input File Parameters Parsed**:
- `tolerance`: Required minimum distance between molecules [testing/runtests.jl:43]()
- `output`: Required output filename [testing/runtests.jl:44]()
- `precision`: Optional, defaults to 0.01 [testing/runtests.jl:45]()
- `pbc`: Optional, can specify 3 values (box size) or 6 values (min/max bounds) [testing/runtests.jl:46-53]()

Sources: [testing/runtests.jl:6-56](), [testing/input_files/toy_with_fixed.inp:1-27]()

## Test Execution Environment Setup

The test environment requires Julia with specific package dependencies:

```mermaid
graph TD
    INSTALL_SH["install_julia.sh<br/>Lines 1-9"] --> CHECK_JULIAUP{"juliaup exists?"}
    CHECK_JULIAUP -->|Yes| SKIP["Use existing Julia"]
    CHECK_JULIAUP -->|No| DOWNLOAD["curl install.julialang.org<br/>Download juliaup.sh"]
    DOWNLOAD --> CHMOD["chmod +x juliaup.sh"]
    CHMOD --> INSTALL["./juliaup.sh -y<br/>Install Julia"]
    
    SKIP --> RUNTESTS_INIT
    INSTALL --> RUNTESTS_INIT
    
    RUNTESTS_INIT["runtests.jl Initialization<br/>Lines 1-2"] --> PKG_ACTIVATE["Pkg.activate(@__DIR__)<br/>Activate test environment"]
    PKG_ACTIVATE --> PKG_INSTALL["Pkg.instantiate()<br/>Install dependencies"]
    
    PKG_INSTALL --> DEPS["Project.toml Dependencies<br/>PDBTools.jl<br/>CellListMap.jl"]
```

**Dependencies** [testing/Project.toml:1-4]():
- `PDBTools`: Parse and manipulate PDB files
- `CellListMap`: Efficient O(N) distance calculations with cell lists

Sources: [testing/install_julia.sh:1-9](), [testing/runtests.jl:1-4](), [testing/Project.toml:1-4]()

# Page: Julia Test Suite

# Julia Test Suite

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [.github/workflows/actions.yml](.github/workflows/actions.yml)
- [testing/Project.toml](testing/Project.toml)
- [testing/input_files/bilayer_pbc.inp](testing/input_files/bilayer_pbc.inp)
- [testing/input_files/mixture_pbc.inp](testing/input_files/mixture_pbc.inp)
- [testing/input_files/protein_outside_pbc_error.inp](testing/input_files/protein_outside_pbc_error.inp)
- [testing/input_files/toy_with_fixed.inp](testing/input_files/toy_with_fixed.inp)
- [testing/input_files/water_box_pbc2.inp](testing/input_files/water_box_pbc2.inp)
- [testing/input_files/water_box_pbc_outside_box.inp](testing/input_files/water_box_pbc_outside_box.inp)
- [testing/install_julia.sh](testing/install_julia.sh)
- [testing/runtests.jl](testing/runtests.jl)
- [testing/test.sh](testing/test.sh)

</details>



## Purpose and Scope

The Julia Test Suite is Packmol's primary validation layer that performs deep structural analysis of generated molecular packings. It executes Packmol, parses the output PDB files, and validates that inter-molecular minimum distances meet specified tolerance requirements within numerical precision bounds. This test suite uses the PDBTools.jl library for PDB parsing and CellListMap.jl for efficient O(N) distance calculations with periodic boundary condition support.

For information about shell-based CLI and error handling tests, see [Shell Test Scripts](#5.2). For the overall CI/CD orchestration, see [Continuous Integration](#5.3).

## Architecture Overview

The Julia test infrastructure consists of three main components: a test orchestrator script, a minimum distance validation function, and a collection of input test cases spanning basic scenarios to complex biological systems.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Test Orchestration"
        test_sh["test.sh<br/>Shell orchestrator"]
        install_julia["install_julia.sh<br/>Julia setup"]
        julia_exe["~/.juliaup/bin/julia<br/>Julia executable"]
    end
    
    subgraph "runtests.jl [Core Test Runner]"
        main_loop["Main loop: for input_test in ARGS"]
        run_packmol["run(pipeline(`packmol`;<br/>stdin=input_test, stdout=log))"]
        success_check["occursin('Success!', String(take!(log)))"]
        check_mind_call["check_mind(input_test)"]
    end
    
    subgraph "check_mind Function [Validator]"
        parse_input["Parse input file:<br/>- tolerance keyword<br/>- output keyword<br/>- pbc keyword<br/>- precision keyword"]
        read_pdb["readPDB(output_name)<br/>PDBTools.jl"]
        create_sys["ParticleSystem(<br/>positions, unitcell,<br/>cutoff, output)"]
        map_pairwise["map_pairwise(<br/>update_mind, sys)"]
        validate["mind.d >= (1-precision)*tolerance"]
    end
    
    subgraph "MinimumDistance [Data Structure]"
        mind_struct["struct MinimumDistance<br/>i: Int (atom index)<br/>j: Int (atom index)<br/>d: Float64 (distance)"]
        update_mind["update_mind(i, j, d2, pdb, md)<br/>Skip same residue<br/>Update if d < md.d"]
        reducer["CellListMap.reducer<br/>Select minimum"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Test Input Files"
        basic["water_box.inp<br/>mixture.inp<br/>spherical.inp"]
        pbc["water_box_pbc*.inp<br/>bilayer_pbc.inp<br/>solvprotein_pbc.inp"]
        complex["bilayer.inp<br/>solvprotein.inp<br/>toy_with_fixed.inp"]
        edge["ieee_signaling.inp<br/>only_one_fixed.inp"]
    end
    
    test_sh --> install_julia
    install_julia --> julia_exe
    test_sh --> main_loop
    julia_exe --> main_loop
    
    main_loop --> run_packmol
    run_packmol --> success_check
    success_check -->|"Success!"| check_mind_call
    success_check -->|No success| error["error('Failed packing')"]
    
    check_mind_call --> parse_input
    parse_input --> read_pdb
    read_pdb --> create_sys
    create_sys --> map_pairwise
    map_pairwise --> update_mind
    update_mind --> reducer
    reducer --> mind_struct
    mind_struct --> validate
    validate -->|Pass| ok["printstyled(' OK.', color=:green)"]
    validate -->|Fail| error_mind["error('minimum distance not correct')"]
    
    basic --> main_loop
    pbc --> main_loop
    complex --> main_loop
    edge --> main_loop
    
    style main_loop fill:#f9f9f9
    style check_mind_call fill:#f9f9f9
    style map_pairwise fill:#f9f9f9
    style validate fill:#f9f9f9
```

**Sources:** [testing/test.sh:1-35](), [testing/runtests.jl:1-109](), [testing/install_julia.sh:1-9]()

## Test Execution Flow

### Test Orchestration

The test suite is launched by `test.sh`, which sets up the Julia environment and invokes `runtests.jl` with a list of input files to test.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant CI as GitHub Actions
    participant test_sh as test.sh
    participant install as install_julia.sh
    participant juliaup as juliaup
    participant runtests as runtests.jl
    participant packmol as packmol binary
    
    CI->>test_sh: Execute ./test.sh
    test_sh->>install: ./install_julia.sh
    install->>juliaup: Check if juliaup exists
    alt juliaup not found
        install->>juliaup: curl install.julialang.org
        install->>juliaup: ./juliaup.sh -y
    end
    
    test_sh->>runtests: $julia_exe runtests.jl [input files...]
    Note over runtests: Parse -packmol argument<br/>Default: ../packmol
    
    loop For each input file
        runtests->>packmol: run(pipeline(`packmol`; stdin=input_file))
        packmol-->>runtests: stdout log
        runtests->>runtests: Check for "Success!" in log
        alt Success found
            runtests->>runtests: check_mind(input_file)
        else No success
            runtests->>runtests: error("Failed packing")
        end
    end
    
    runtests-->>test_sh: Exit status
    test_sh-->>CI: Test results
```

The test script accepts an optional `-packmol` argument to specify the path to the Packmol executable. If not provided, it defaults to `../packmol` relative to the testing directory.

**Sources:** [testing/test.sh:5-24](), [testing/runtests.jl:81-106]()

### Input File Coverage

The test suite covers 17 distinct input files representing various molecular packing scenarios:

| Category | Input Files | Purpose |
|----------|-------------|---------|
| Basic Systems | `water_box.inp`, `mixture.inp`, `spherical.inp` | Simple packings without PBC |
| Periodic Boundary | `water_box_pbc.inp`, `water_box_pbc2.inp`, `mixture_pbc.inp` | Standard PBC configurations |
| PBC Edge Cases | `water_box_pbc_negative_coordinates.inp`, `water_box_pbc_outside_box.inp`, `water_box_pbc_slab.inp` | Negative coords, outside box, slab geometry |
| Complex Biological | `bilayer.inp`, `bilayer_pbc.inp`, `solvprotein.inp`, `solvprotein_pbc.inp` | Lipid bilayers, solvated proteins |
| Fixed Molecules | `toy_with_fixed.inp`, `only_one_fixed.inp` | Systems with fixed molecular positions |
| Numerical Edge Cases | `ieee_signaling.inp`, `spherical_pbc.inp` | IEEE floating-point handling, spherical constraints with PBC |

**Sources:** [testing/test.sh:8-24]()

## Minimum Distance Validation

### The `check_mind` Function

The core validation logic is implemented in the `check_mind` function, which performs a multi-step validation process:

```mermaid
graph TB
    start["check_mind(input_file)"] --> init["Initialize:<br/>tolerance = nothing<br/>output_name = nothing<br/>unitcell = nothing<br/>precision = 0.01"]
    
    init --> parse_loop["Parse input file line by line"]
    
    parse_loop --> extract_tol["Extract 'tolerance' value"]
    parse_loop --> extract_out["Extract 'output' filename"]
    parse_loop --> extract_prec["Extract 'precision' value<br/>(default: 0.01)"]
    parse_loop --> extract_pbc["Extract 'pbc' parameters"]
    
    extract_pbc --> pbc_3["3 values → pbc 0 0 0 lx ly lz<br/>unitcell = [lx, ly, lz]"]
    extract_pbc --> pbc_6["6 values → pbc x0 y0 z0 x1 y1 z1<br/>unitcell = [x1-x0, y1-y0, z1-z0]"]
    
    extract_tol --> validate_parsed["Validate tolerance and<br/>output_name exist"]
    extract_out --> validate_parsed
    extract_prec --> validate_parsed
    pbc_3 --> validate_parsed
    pbc_6 --> validate_parsed
    
    validate_parsed -->|Missing| error_parse["error('tolerance or output not found')"]
    validate_parsed -->|Valid| read["readPDB(output_name)<br/>PDBTools.jl"]
    
    read --> create_sys["ParticleSystem(<br/>positions = coor.(pdb),<br/>unitcell = unitcell,<br/>cutoff = tolerance * 1.5,<br/>output = MinimumDistance(0,0,+Inf))"]
    
    create_sys --> map["mind = map_pairwise(<br/>(x,y,i,j,d2,md) → update_mind(i,j,d2,pdb,md),<br/>sys)"]
    
    map --> check["mind.d >= (1-precision)*tolerance"]
    
    check -->|Fail| error_dist["error('minimum distance not correct<br/>Obtained: mind.d<br/>Expected: >= (1-precision)*tolerance<br/>Atoms: mind.i and mind.j')"]
    
    check -->|Pass| success["printstyled(' OK.', color=:green, bold=true)"]
    
    style create_sys fill:#f9f9f9
    style map fill:#f9f9f9
    style check fill:#f9f9f9
```

**Sources:** [testing/runtests.jl:34-78]()

### Input File Parsing

The function parses the input file to extract key parameters:

- **`tolerance`**: The minimum allowed inter-molecular distance
- **`output`**: The output PDB filename to validate
- **`precision`**: Tolerance precision factor (default: 0.01 if not specified)
- **`pbc`**: Periodic boundary condition box dimensions

The PBC parameter can be specified in two formats:
- 3 values: `pbc lx ly lz` (box from origin)
- 6 values: `pbc x0 y0 z0 x1 y1 z1` (explicit box bounds)

**Sources:** [testing/runtests.jl:39-55]()

### Distance Calculation with CellListMap

The minimum distance calculation leverages the CellListMap.jl library, which provides O(N) scaling through cell list spatial partitioning. The system is configured with:

| Parameter | Value | Purpose |
|-----------|-------|---------|
| `positions` | `coor.(pdb)` | Cartesian coordinates from PDB file |
| `unitcell` | Parsed from `pbc` keyword | Box dimensions for PBC wrapping |
| `cutoff` | `tolerance * 1.5` | Interaction cutoff radius |
| `output` | `MinimumDistance(0, 0, +Inf)` | Initial output structure |

The `map_pairwise` function efficiently computes pairwise interactions by only evaluating atom pairs within the cutoff distance, automatically handling periodic boundary conditions when `unitcell` is specified.

**Sources:** [testing/runtests.jl:59-66]()

## MinimumDistance Data Structure

### Custom Type Definition

The validation uses a custom `MinimumDistance` struct to track the closest inter-molecular approach:

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class MinimumDistance {
        +Int i
        +Int j
        +Float64 d
    }
    
    class CellListMapIntegration {
        <<interface>>
        +update_mind(i, j, d2, pdb, md)
        +reducer(md1, md2)
        +copy_output(md)
        +reset_output(md)
    }
    
    MinimumDistance ..|> CellListMapIntegration : implements
    
    note for MinimumDistance "i, j: Atom indices (1-based)\nd: Distance in Angstroms"
    note for CellListMapIntegration "CellListMap.jl requires these functions\nto support custom reduction operations"
```

**Sources:** [testing/runtests.jl:20-32]()

### Custom Reduction Operations

The `MinimumDistance` type integrates with CellListMap through four required functions:

#### `update_mind`

This function is called for each atom pair within the cutoff distance:

```
function update_mind(i, j, d2, pdb, md::MinimumDistance)
    residue(pdb[i]) == residue(pdb[j]) && return md  # Skip intra-molecular
    d = sqrt(d2)
    return d < md.d ? MinimumDistance(i, j, d) : md  # Keep minimum
end
```

The function skips atom pairs from the same residue (intra-molecular distances) since the validation only concerns inter-molecular spacing. This relies on the PDB structure having distinct residue identifiers for each molecule, which is ensured by the `resnumbers` option in Packmol input files.

**Sources:** [testing/runtests.jl:25-29](), [testing/runtests.jl:6-12]()

#### Reducer Functions

The remaining three functions enable CellListMap's parallel reduction:

| Function | Purpose | Implementation |
|----------|---------|----------------|
| `reducer(md1, md2)` | Combine results from parallel threads | Return `md1.d < md2.d ? md1 : md2` |
| `copy_output(md)` | Create independent copy for thread safety | Return `md` (immutable struct) |
| `reset_output(md)` | Initialize accumulator for each thread | Return `MinimumDistance(0, 0, +Inf)` |

**Sources:** [testing/runtests.jl:30-32]()

## Validation Criteria

### Precision-Based Tolerance

The validation checks that the computed minimum distance meets the tolerance with a precision allowance:

```
mind.d >= (1 - precision) * tolerance
```

| Parameter | Typical Value | Source |
|-----------|---------------|--------|
| `tolerance` | 2.0 Å | Input file `tolerance` keyword |
| `precision` | 0.01 (1%) | Input file `precision` keyword or default |
| Threshold | 1.98 Å | `(1 - 0.01) * 2.0` |

This precision allowance accounts for numerical artifacts in the optimization and floating-point arithmetic. If the minimum distance falls below the threshold, the test fails with a detailed error message including:

- The input file name
- Obtained minimum distance
- Expected threshold
- Atom indices (both 1-based Julia indexing and 0-based VMD indexing)

**Sources:** [testing/runtests.jl:67-75]()

### Success Message Verification

Before running minimum distance validation, the test suite verifies that Packmol reported successful completion by searching for the string `"Success!"` in the execution log. If this message is not found, the test fails immediately without attempting validation.

**Sources:** [testing/runtests.jl:96-100]()

## Dependency Management

### Julia Package Environment

The test suite uses a local Julia environment defined by `Project.toml`:

```mermaid
graph LR
    Project["Project.toml<br/>testing/Project.toml"]
    PDBTools["PDBTools.jl<br/>e29189f1-7114-4dbd-93d0-c5673a921a58"]
    CellListMap["CellListMap.jl<br/>69e1c6dd-3888-40e6-b3c8-31ac5f578864"]
    
    Project --> PDBTools
    Project --> CellListMap
    
    PDBTools -.->|Parse PDB files| readPDB["readPDB()<br/>coor()<br/>residue()"]
    CellListMap -.->|Distance calc| ParticleSystem["ParticleSystem<br/>map_pairwise"]
    
    style Project fill:#f9f9f9
    style readPDB fill:#f9f9f9
    style ParticleSystem fill:#f9f9f9
```

The environment is activated and instantiated at the beginning of `runtests.jl`:

```julia
import Pkg; Pkg.activate(@__DIR__); Pkg.instantiate()
```

This ensures all dependencies are available before running tests.

**Sources:** [testing/runtests.jl:1-4](), [testing/Project.toml:1-4]()

## Integration with Test Suite

### Invocation Pattern

The Julia test suite is invoked from `test.sh` after the Packmol binary is compiled:

```bash
julia_exe=~/.juliaup/bin/julia
$julia_exe runtests.jl ./input_files/water_box.inp \
                      ./input_files/mixture.inp \
                      # ... (17 total input files)
```

Each input file path is passed as a command-line argument, and `runtests.jl` processes them sequentially.

**Sources:** [testing/test.sh:5-24]()

### CI/CD Integration

The GitHub Actions workflow compiles Packmol using both `make` and `cmake`, then runs the test suite on both Ubuntu and macOS:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant GH as GitHub Actions
    participant Compile as Compile Step
    participant CD as cd testing
    participant Install as install_julia.sh
    participant Test as test.sh
    participant Julia as runtests.jl
    
    GH->>Compile: make or cmake
    Compile->>CD: cd testing
    CD->>Install: ./install_julia.sh
    Install-->>CD: Julia ready
    CD->>Test: ./test.sh
    Test->>Julia: Run 17 test cases
    Julia-->>Test: All tests pass/fail
    Test-->>GH: Exit status
```

The workflow tests on multiple platforms and compilers to ensure cross-platform compatibility.

**Sources:** [.github/workflows/actions.yml:1-46]()

## Periodic Boundary Condition Handling

### PBC Parameter Extraction

When the input file contains a `pbc` keyword, the validator extracts box dimensions and passes them to CellListMap:

```mermaid
graph TD
    pbc_line["pbc keyword in input file"]
    
    pbc_line --> check_length{"Length of values"}
    
    check_length -->|3 values| format1["pbc lx ly lz<br/>(box from origin)"]
    check_length -->|6 values| format2["pbc x0 y0 z0 x1 y1 z1<br/>(explicit bounds)"]
    check_length -->|Other| error["error('pbc not properly set')"]
    
    format1 --> calc1["unitcell = [lx, ly, lz]"]
    format2 --> calc2["unitcell = [x1-x0, y1-y0, z1-z0]"]
    
    calc1 --> pass_to_sys["ParticleSystem(<br/>unitcell = unitcell)"]
    calc2 --> pass_to_sys
    
    pass_to_sys --> celllist["CellListMap handles<br/>PBC distance wrapping"]
    
    style pass_to_sys fill:#f9f9f9
    style celllist fill:#f9f9f9
```

When `unitcell` is provided to `ParticleSystem`, CellListMap automatically applies minimum image convention for distance calculations, ensuring correct validation for periodic systems.

**Sources:** [testing/runtests.jl:46-54]()

## Error Reporting

### Failure Message Format

When validation fails, the error message provides comprehensive debugging information:

```
Packing reported success, but minimum distance is not correct for $input_file
Obtained minimum-distance = $(mind.d) for tolerance $tolerance and precision $precision.
Atoms: $(mind.i) and $(mind.j) - VMD: index $(mind.i-1) $(mind.j-1)
```

The message includes both 1-based Julia indexing and 0-based VMD indexing to facilitate visualization and debugging in molecular visualization tools.

**Sources:** [testing/runtests.jl:68-74]()

### Test Isolation

Each test case runs independently. If one test fails, the error is immediately reported and the test suite terminates due to the `set -e` flag in `test.sh`. This fail-fast behavior ensures that test failures are noticed and addressed promptly.

**Sources:** [testing/test.sh:3-4]()

# Shell Test Scripts

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [.github/workflows/actions.yml](.github/workflows/actions.yml)
